questions.q: The prime number theorem is the statement that, as $x \to \infty$,
questions.hint: Primes thin out logarithmically: roughly one in $\log x$ integers near $x$ is prime.
questions.explain: PNT says $\pi(x)/(x/\log x) \to 1$. Equivalently $\pi(x) \sim \mathrm{Li}(x)$, which is a numerically tighter approximation.

questions.q: Which of $\pi(x)$, $x/\log x$, $\mathrm{Li}(x)$ is the closest numerical approximation to $\pi(x)$ for moderate $x$ (say $x = 10^9$)?
questions.hint: $\mathrm{Li}(x) = \int_2^x dt/\log t$ matches the harmonic-density heuristic better than $x/\log x$.
questions.explain: $\mathrm{Li}(x)$ has the same leading term as $x/\log x$ but absorbs the correction $x/(\log x)^2 + \cdots$, so it tracks $\pi(x)$ much more tightly.

questions.q: $\pi(100) = ?$ (the number of primes up to $100$)
questions.explain: There are $25$ primes $\le 100$. The PNT estimate $100/\log 100 \approx 21.7$, while $\mathrm{Li}(100) \approx 30.1$ — both are in the right ballpark.

questions.q: Which of these directly links the non-trivial zeros of $\zeta(s)$ to the prime-counting error?
choices: The von Mangoldt explicit formula $\psi(x) = x - \sum_\rho x^\rho/\rho - \log 2\pi - \tfrac12\log(1-x^{-2})$
questions.hint: The explicit formula sums $x^\rho/\rho$ over zeros $\rho$.
questions.explain: Apply Perron's formula to $-\zeta'/\zeta$: shifting the contour past the non-trivial zeros picks up a residue $-x^\rho/\rho$ at each, and the trivial pole at $s=1$ contributes $+x$.

questions.q: The Riemann hypothesis ($\mathrm{Re}\,\rho = 1/2$ for every non-trivial zero $\rho$) is equivalent to which sharpening of PNT?
questions.hint: Each zero $\rho$ contributes a term $x^\rho/\rho$; if all $\rho$ have real part $1/2$ the total is $O(x^{1/2}\cdot \#\{\text{zeros up to height }T\})$.
questions.explain: RH is equivalent to $\psi(x) - x \ll x^{1/2}(\log x)^2$. This is the sharpest possible error, because zeros on the critical line force at least $x^{1/2}$ oscillation.

questions.q: The unique pole of $\zeta(s)$ in $\mathbb{C}$ is simple and located at $s = ?$
questions.hint: It is the value of $s$ at which the harmonic series $\sum 1/n$ would diverge.
questions.explain: $\zeta(s)$ has a simple pole with residue $1$ at $s = 1$; the explicit formula's leading term $+x$ in $\psi(x)$ comes from this pole.

questions.q: Hadamard and de la Vallée Poussin's proof of PNT (1896) hinges on which property of $\zeta(s)$?
choices: $\zeta(s)$ has no zeros on the line $\mathrm{Re}\,s = 1$
$\zeta(s)$ has only finitely many zeros in the critical strip
questions.hint: Pushing a zero off the line $\mathrm{Re}\,s = 1$ is the analytic content of PNT.
questions.explain: The classical proof uses the inequality $3 + 4\cos\theta + \cos 2\theta \ge 0$ applied to $|\zeta(\sigma)^3 \zeta(\sigma + it)^4 \zeta(\sigma + 2it)|$ to rule out $\zeta(1+it) = 0$.

questions.q: The classical zero-free region pushes $\zeta$'s zeros into
choices: $\sigma > 1$ (no zeros to the right of the line)
questions.hint: It is a thin sliver to the left of $\sigma = 1$ that narrows as $|t| \to \infty$.
questions.explain: The de la Vallée Poussin region is $\sigma > 1 - c/\log|t|$, narrowing logarithmically; combined with the explicit formula it gives PNT with error $O(x e^{-c\sqrt{\log x}})$.

questions.q: Improving the zero-free region from $\sigma > 1 - c/\log|t|$ to $\sigma > 1/2$ would imply
choices: Dirichlet's theorem on primes in AP
the Riemann hypothesis (and the optimal PNT remainder)
questions.hint: The zero-free region's right edge is the location of the rightmost zero.
questions.explain: Pushing all non-trivial zeros to $\sigma \le 1/2$ is RH; via the explicit formula this yields $\psi(x) - x = O(x^{1/2}(\log x)^2)$.

ant-dirichlet-theorem.title: Dirichlet's theorem on primes in AP

questions.q: Dirichlet's theorem (1837) states that for $\gcd(a, q) = 1$, the progression $a, a+q, a+2q, \ldots$ contains
choices: primes only when $q$ is itself prime
questions.hint: It is a qualitative, not asymptotic, statement.
questions.explain: Dirichlet showed there are infinitely many primes $\equiv a \pmod q$ whenever $\gcd(a, q) = 1$. The quantitative refinement $\pi(x; q, a) \sim \frac{1}{\varphi(q)} x/\log x$ is PNT for APs.

questions.q: The crucial analytic input in Dirichlet's proof is
questions.hint: If $L(1, \chi) = 0$ for some $\chi$, the prime sums over the progression would not diverge.
questions.explain: Orthogonality $\frac{1}{\varphi(q)} \sum_\chi \bar\chi(a) \chi(p) = \mathbf 1_{p \equiv a}$ converts $\sum_{p \equiv a} p^{-s}$ into a sum over $\log L(s, \chi)$. Each non-trivial $L(s, \chi)$ stays finite at $s = 1$ provided $L(1, \chi) \ne 0$, and the trivial character contributes the $\log \zeta(s)$ blow-up.

questions.q: How many residue classes $a \bmod 12$ with $\gcd(a, 12) = 1$ are there? (This is $\varphi(12)$, the number of primes-in-AP classes mod 12.)
questions.hint: List units mod 12: $1, 5, 7, 11$.
questions.explain: $\varphi(12) = \varphi(4)\varphi(3) = 2 \cdot 2 = 4$. Each class $1, 5, 7, 11 \pmod{12}$ contains $\sim x/(4 \log x)$ primes up to $x$.

questions.q: Naive Möbius-weighted inclusion–exclusion $\sum_{d \mid P(z)} \mu(d) \lfloor x/d \rfloor$ counts integers up to $x$ with no prime factor $\le z$. Why does it fail to count primes directly?
choices: The Möbius function is undefined on primes
The error term grows like $2^{\pi(z)}$ when $z$ approaches $\sqrt{x}$, swamping the main term
It only counts prime powers, not primes
It always gives a negative answer
questions.hint: The sum has $2^{\pi(z)}$ terms, each contributing an $O(1)$ error.
questions.explain: Each $\lfloor x/d \rfloor$ has error $O(1)$, and there are $2^{\pi(z)}$ divisors of $P(z) = \prod_{p \le z} p$. Truncating the sum at small $d$ (Brun, Selberg) is the modern fix.

questions.q: Brun's sieve famously gives which conditional twin-prime result?
choices: There are infinitely many twin primes
There are no twin primes above $10^{18}$
questions.hint: Convergence of the reciprocal sum is the celebrated 1919 Brun bound.
questions.explain: Brun (1919) proved $\#\{p \le x : p, p+2 \text{ both prime}\} \ll x/(\log x)^2$, which makes the reciprocal sum converge to Brun's constant $B_2 \approx 1.902\ldots$ — strikingly, this stops short of proving infinitude either way.

questions.q: The Selberg upper-bound sieve finds the optimal weights $\lambda_d$ in
questions.hint: Squares are non-negative, so the LHS is an automatic upper bound for any indicator-truncation of the divisor sum.
questions.explain: Selberg's $\Lambda^2$ trick: $\bigl(\sum_{d \mid n} \lambda_d\bigr)^2 \ge 1$ whenever $\lambda_1 = 1$, so the squared sum is an upper bound. Optimizing $\lambda$ subject to $\lambda_d = 0$ for $d > z$ becomes a quadratic program with a clean closed form.

questions.q: The Bombieri–Vinogradov theorem (1965) bounds $\sum_{q \le Q} \max_{\gcd(a,q)=1} |\pi(x;q,a) - \mathrm{Li}(x)/\varphi(q)|$ for which range of $Q$?
questions.hint: The barrier is $Q \le \sqrt{x}$, the same threshold GRH would yield individually.
questions.explain: Bombieri–Vinogradov works up to $Q \le x^{1/2}/(\log x)^A$ and gives a bound $\ll x/(\log x)^B$. This is GRH-quality on average — pushing $Q$ past $x^{1/2}$ is the Elliott–Halberstam conjecture.

questions.q: Why is Bombieri–Vinogradov as strong as GRH for many applications?
choices: Most arithmetic applications only need an average bound over moduli, not a pointwise bound for each $q$
It eliminates the need for sieve weights
questions.hint: Sieve and prime-distribution arguments typically sum errors over $q$, so $\ell^1$-on-average is the relevant norm.
questions.explain: Many sieve applications (e.g. Chen's theorem, twin almost-primes, bounded gaps) need $\sum_q E(x; q, a)$ small, not each individual $E(x; q, a)$. Bombieri–Vinogradov supplies exactly that, hence the slogan 'GRH on average'.

questions.q: The Elliott–Halberstam conjecture extends Bombieri–Vinogradov by allowing
choices: moduli that are prime powers only
questions.hint: It pushes the cutoff from $\sqrt{x}$ to nearly $x$.
questions.explain: Elliott–Halberstam (1968) conjectures the same average bound holds for $Q \le x^{1-\varepsilon}$. Conditional on it, sieve methods give bounded prime gaps as small as $12$ (Maynard); Zhang's unconditional gap of $70 \cdot 10^6$ used a weakened EH result.

questions.q: In the circle method, the count $r_k(N)$ of representations of $N$ as a sum of $k$ values of $f$ is recovered as which integral over the generating exponential sum $S(\alpha) = \sum_n e(\alpha f(n))$?
questions.hint: Multiplying by $e(-N\alpha)$ and integrating extracts the Fourier coefficient at $N$.
questions.explain: $S(\alpha)^k = \sum_{n_1,\ldots,n_k} e(\alpha\,(f(n_1)+\cdots+f(n_k)))$, and $\int_0^1 e(\alpha m)\,d\alpha = \mathbf 1_{m=0}$, so $\int_0^1 S(\alpha)^k e(-N\alpha)\,d\alpha$ counts solutions to $f(n_1)+\cdots+f(n_k)=N$.

questions.q: On the major arcs (the union of small neighborhoods of rationals $a/q$ with $q$ small), the exponential sum $S(\alpha)$ behaves like
choices: a clean main term $\frac{1}{q}\,c_q(a) \cdot v(\alpha - a/q)$ from a singular series, plus a controllable error
a rapidly oscillating noise indistinguishable from white noise
questions.hint: Near $a/q$, the integers $n$ split into residue classes mod $q$, giving a Ramanujan-type sum $c_q(a) = \sum_{(t,q)=1} e(at/q)$ and a smooth integral $v$.
questions.explain: The major-arc analysis writes $S(\alpha)$ near $a/q$ in terms of a Gauss/Ramanujan sum (the arithmetic factor $c_q(a)/q$) times a smooth oscillatory integral $v(\alpha - a/q)$ that contains the analytic content. Summing these contributions across rationals gives the singular series — the heuristic main term.

questions.q: The Hardy–Littlewood prediction for $r_3(N) = \#\{(p_1,p_2,p_3): p_1+p_2+p_3 = N, \text{ each } p_i \text{ prime}\}$ has main term $\mathfrak{S}(N) \cdot N^2/(2\,(\log N)^3)$ for odd $N$. For even $N$, the singular series $\mathfrak{S}(N)$ vanishes; what is its value?
questions.hint: An even number is a sum of three odd primes only if one of them is $2$, which is rare; the local obstruction at $2$ kills $\mathfrak{S}$.
questions.explain: Three odd primes always sum to an odd number, so $\mathfrak{S}(N) = 0$ for even $N$. This is the local obstruction at $p=2$. For odd $N$, $\mathfrak{S}(N) \ge \mathfrak{S}_0 > 0$, and Vinogradov's theorem says ternary Goldbach holds for every sufficiently large odd $N$ (now every odd $N \ge 7$, by Helfgott).

questions.q: Weyl's criterion characterizes equidistribution of $\{a_n\} \subset \mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z}$ as the condition that, for every nonzero integer $k$,
questions.hint: Equidistribution is dual to cancellation in every nonzero Fourier mode.
questions.explain: By Weierstrass, equidistribution of $\{a_n\}$ on the circle is equivalent to $\frac{1}{N}\sum f(a_n) \to \int f$ for every continuous $f$. Trigonometric polynomials are dense, so it reduces to the single-frequency condition $\frac{1}{N}\sum e(k a_n) \to 0$ for $k \ne 0$.

questions.q: Why is $\{n\alpha\}_{n=1}^\infty$ equidistributed on $[0,1)$ exactly when $\alpha$ is irrational?
choices: Rational $\alpha$ makes the sequence periodic, so it samples only finitely many values
Rational $\alpha$ violates Weyl's criterion only for $k = 0$
questions.hint: If $\alpha = p/q$, the sequence cycles with period $q$.
questions.explain: For rational $\alpha = p/q$, $\{n\alpha\}$ takes only finitely many values $0, 1/q, \ldots, (q-1)/q$, so $\frac{1}{N}\sum e(k n\alpha)$ does not vanish for $k$ a multiple of $q$. For irrational $\alpha$ the geometric sum $\sum_{n=1}^N e(k n\alpha) = (e(k(N+1)\alpha) - e(k\alpha))/(e(k\alpha)-1)$ is bounded by $1/|\sin \pi k\alpha|$, so $1/N$ times it tends to $0$ — Weyl's criterion holds.

questions.q: Weyl's inequality bounds $\bigl|\sum_{n \le N} e(\alpha n^k)\bigr|$ when $\alpha$ has a rational approximation $|\alpha - a/q| < 1/q^2$, $\gcd(a,q)=1$. The key consequence is
choices: the sum is $\ll N (q^{-1} + N^{-1} + qN^{-k})^{1/2^{k-1}}$, so it is small unless $q$ is in a narrow range
the sum has size $\sqrt{N}$ regardless of $\alpha$
questions.hint: Weyl's inequality is what makes the minor-arc bound in the circle method work — the exponent $1/2^{k-1}$ is small but nontrivial.
questions.explain: Weyl's inequality gives $|\sum_{n \le N} e(\alpha n^k)| \ll N^{1+\varepsilon} (q^{-1} + N^{-1} + qN^{-k})^{1/2^{k-1}}$, which is nontrivial when $q$ is neither too small (then $\alpha$ is on a major arc) nor too large (then $qN^{-k}$ dominates). The $1/2^{k-1}$ savings degrade with $k$, motivating Vinogradov's mean-value theorem for sharper bounds.

ant-selberg-elementary.title: Selberg's symmetry formula and elementary PNT

questions.q: Selberg's symmetry formula reads
choices: $\sum_{p \le x} \log^2 p + \sum_{pq \le x} \log p \log q = 2 x \log x + O(x)$
questions.hint: It is symmetric in primes ($p$) and prime pairs ($pq$).
questions.explain: Selberg derived $\sum_{p \le x} \log^2 p + \sum_{pq \le x} \log p \log q = 2 x \log x + O(x)$ by elementary manipulations of $\Lambda * 1 = \log$ and $\Lambda + \Lambda * \Lambda$. The two sums are forced to balance: if one is too small the other must be too large, leading to a contradiction unless both behave like $x \log x$.

questions.q: Why was the elementary proof of PNT (Erdős–Selberg, 1948–49) historically significant?
choices: It gave a sharper error term than Hadamard's analytic proof
It showed that complex analysis is not strictly necessary for PNT, contrary to what was widely believed
It eliminated the need to define $\pi(x)$
It generalized PNT to infinite-dimensional algebras
questions.hint: Hardy and others had conjectured no elementary proof was possible.
questions.explain: Hardy had publicly speculated that PNT could not be proved without complex analysis, viewing the depth of the result as inseparable from the analytic structure of $\zeta(s)$. The Erdős–Selberg argument refuted this — though the resulting error term is weaker than the analytic proof's $O(x e^{-c\sqrt{\log x}})$, the proof is essentially real-variable.

questions.q: The bootstrap from Selberg's symmetry formula to PNT proceeds by
choices: showing that $A = \limsup_x |\psi(x)/x - 1|$ satisfies $A \le \tfrac12 A$ (so $A = 0$), via the symmetry's averaging effect
induction on the number of prime factors
questions.hint: Symmetry feeds back the same quantity at half scale — a self-improvement loop forces zero.
questions.explain: Define $R(x) = \psi(x) - x$. Selberg's formula combined with elementary inequalities gives $|R(x)| \le \tfrac{1}{2}\max_{y \le x} |R(y)| + o(x)$, which iterates down to $R(x) = o(x)$ — i.e. $\psi(x) \sim x$, equivalent to PNT. The averaging on the right is the symmetric pairing of $p$ with $pq$.

questions.q: The (analytic) large sieve inequality bounds
choices: $\sum_{q \le Q} \sum_{\chi \bmod q}^{*} \bigl|\sum_{n \le N} a_n \chi(n)\bigr|^2 \le (Q^2 + N) \sum_{n \le N} |a_n|^2$
questions.hint: Sum is over $q \le Q$ and primitive characters $\chi^*$ mod $q$; the constant is $Q^2 + N$.
questions.explain: The Montgomery–Bombieri form of the large sieve says $\sum_{q \le Q} \sum_{\chi^*} |\sum_{n \le N} a_n \chi(n)|^2 \le (Q^2 + N)\|a\|_2^2$. The dual form bounds $\sum_r |\sum_n a_n e(n\alpha_r)|^2$ by $(\delta^{-1}+N)\|a\|_2^2$ for $\delta$-spaced frequencies $\alpha_r$ — the two are equivalent via Plancherel.

questions.q: The large sieve constant $(Q^2 + N)$ is essentially sharp because
choices: the number of primitive characters $\sum_{q \le Q}\varphi^*(q) \sim Q^2/\zeta(2)$, and the inequality is tight when $a_n$ is supported on a residue class
Riemann's hypothesis would imply a smaller constant
questions.hint: Counting primitive characters mod $q \le Q$ is asymptotic to $Q^2 / \zeta(2)$.
questions.explain: There are $\asymp Q^2$ primitive characters of conductors $\le Q$, so the LHS already has $\asymp Q^2 \|a\|_2^2$ Plancherel mass when $a$ is concentrated on one residue class. The $N$ on the right is the trivial bound from Cauchy–Schwarz applied to a single Dirichlet sum. Both regimes show up — hence $Q^2 + N$, not max.

questions.q: Take $N = 100$ and $a_n = 1$ for $n \le N$, $0$ otherwise. The right-hand side coefficient $\sum_{n \le N} |a_n|^2$ in the large sieve equals what number?
questions.hint: It is just the count of nonzero entries.
questions.explain: $\sum |a_n|^2 = \sum_{n \le 100} 1 = 100$. So with $Q = \sqrt{N} = 10$, the large sieve gives $\sum_{q,\chi^*} |\sum_n \chi(n)|^2 \le (Q^2+N) N = 200 \cdot 100 = 20000$ — substantially sharper than the trivial $\sum_q q \cdot N^2$.
